Prevention: Avoid using seeds from the previous harvest if the crops were infested with
Use certified crop seed to reduce the chance of contamination.
Intercrop with trap crops, like maize, pigeon pea, Mucuna, sorghum, cotton and soyabean to reduce the
Striga seed bank in the soil.
Striga seeds germinate but cannot attach itself to the roots of these crops, so it dies.
Rotate cowpea with non-susceptible crops, such as groundnuts for no less than 3 years as seeds remain in the soil.
Apply organic or inorganic fertilizer (80kg of
N/ha) to improve soil fertility for better crop health and better tolerance to weeds.
Avoid grazing animals or livestock in fields infested with
Seeds are dispersed by water - construct contours and water ways to prevent run-off carrying striga seed from infested land to clean fields.
Clean machinery and equipment used in infested fields before using them in uninfested fields.
Monitoring: Striga witchweed is a small parasitic plant that attaches to, and penetrates the root of cowpea.
Look for purplish or yellow flowering parasitic weeds attached to the crop that grows up to 10-20 cm.
Look for yellowed cowpea leaves or early aging of cowpea plants in the field and search for presence of the
Uprooting infested plants reveals the yellowish
Striga root of 1-3 cm in diameter attaching to the plant.
Do regular plant monitoring and act as soon as possible before the weed flowers.
Direct Control: This should be done before the weed flowers and sets seed.
If you weed late and do not put them in your compost pile or pit, burn the collected plants to kill the seeds since seeds stay for a long time in the soil.
Restrictions: There are no silver bullet control methods for controlling
Management of the weed mainly depends on the cultural practices listed in the prevention.
Use of herbicides usually negatively affects the crops and is not advised.
